title: Greenpeace urges COP17 leaders to treat biodiversity as public duty, not profit
content:
An Lambrechts, a biodiversity politics expert at Greenpeace International and head of the Greenpeace delegation at the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) COP17 in Yerevan, Armenia, argues that protecting nature is a public duty rather than a private profit opportunity. With COP17 marking the halfway point to the 2030 deadline set by the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, the first Global Review indicates that countries are not on track to meet biodiversity targets. Lambrechts notes that while funding is insufficient, the core issue is a public policy distortion where the global economy spends approximately $30 destroying nature for every $1 invested in its protection.

The disparity is highlighted by data from the Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services, which reports $2.4 trillion in public subsidies for fossil fuels, agriculture, and water use, compared to only $220 billion in global investment for biodiversity conservation and restoration. Lambrechts criticizes the current discourse, which suggests that mobilizing private capital, scaling offsets, and “derisking” investments can close the finance gap. She contends that this approach misunderstands ecological stewardship, as biodiversity is a non-monetisable public good essential for human survival, and relying on profit-seeking capital perpetuates the structural drivers of ecosystem destruction.

Instead of seeking private solutions, Lambrechts advocates for recovering public wealth lost to cross-border tax abuse, financial secrecy, and corporate impunity. She urges finance and environment ministers in Yerevan to support swift action on global tax rule reforms, the elimination of harmful subsidies, and the cancellation of unsustainable sovereign debts. In advanced economies, public funding often undermines biodiversity; for instance, Europe funnels over €5.3 billion annually into intensive forest biomass harvesting under renewable energy directives, which degrades primary forest ecosystems.

For developing countries, the reliance on private finance is complicated by a severe sovereign debt crisis. In 2024, public debt in these economies reached record levels, with net interest payments absorbing $921 billion. A record 61 developing countries now spend more than 10% of government revenue on foreign debt service, and many climate-vulnerable nations spend twice as much servicing external debt as they receive in combined climate and biodiversity finance. This financial burden forces governments into austerity measures and the expansion of raw commodity exports into pristine biomes to secure foreign exchange.

Lambrechts points to the United Nations Framework Convention on International Tax Cooperation (UNFCITC) negotiations as a potential path forward, noting that an estimated $492 billion in tax revenue is lost annually to offshore tax havens. Multinational corporations account for approximately $348 billion of this loss by shifting profits away from countries experiencing environmental degradation, with developing nations losing tens of billions annually in the mining sector alone. Additionally, illicit financial flows from illegal logging drain between $51 billion and $152 billion yearly. She concludes that leaders at COP17 must prioritize securing predictable, sufficient, and sovereign public finance for biodiversity conservation to ensure a restorative future.
summary: An Lambrechts is a biodiversity politics expert at Greenpeace International with extensive experience in biodiversity-related multilateral negotiations. She is the head of the Greenpeace delegation at the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) COP17 happening in Yerevan, Armenia.

title: Minns government to introduce bill allowing Mount Pleasant coal output increase of 32%
content:
The Minns government plans to introduce special legislation allowing MACH Energy to increase coal production at its Mount Pleasant coalmine in the New South Wales Hunter Valley. Premier Chris Minns stated the bill would authorize a 32% annual production increase, raising output from 12.5 million tonnes to 16.5 million tonnes per year until 2032. Minns claimed the measure is necessary to save 400 jobs at the site before Christmas.

The proposed legislation has been criticized as “legislative overreach” because the mine is subject to a landmark high court decision. Critics accuse the government of bypassing the ruling by using new laws to permit the production expansion.

title: Tap water no longer drinkable in Norwegian town as climate-related thawing releases heavy metals
content: Warning for other Arctic communities as residents told not to use water in Longyearbyen in Svalbard, one of the fastest-warming places in the world Residents of a remote town in Norway that is in one of the fastest-warming places in the world have been told they must no longer drink tap water due to heavy metal contamination that scientists have linked to the thawing permafrost. Longyearbyen, in the archipelago of Svalbard, gets its main drinking water supply from a 1.5 mile-long (2.5km) dammed lake called Isdammen, or “ice pond”. Higher temperatures as a result of the climate crisis have thawed permafrost, leading to newly exposed bedrock leaching metals into the pond.

title: Study Shows Daily Weather Variability Drives Faster Glacier Ice Loss
content:
A new study led by researchers at ETH Zurich and the Vrije Universiteit Brussel has been published in Nature Communications. The paper shows that glaciers worldwide could lose ice faster than previously projected.

The authors found that incorporating daily weather variability into glacier models produces more realistic melt simulations. This adjustment results in greater projected ice loss by the end of the century compared with earlier estimates that used longer‑term averages.

The research highlights the importance of short‑lived weather events, such as exceptional heat waves and extreme melt seasons that have recently been observed in several glacierized regions around the globe.
summary: Researchers at ETH Zurich and Vrije Universiteit Brussel found that including daily weather variability in glacier models leads to greater projected ice loss by the end of the century. The study, published in Nature Communications, emphasizes the role of short‑lived weather events such as heat waves and extreme melt seasons in accelerating glacier melt.

title: Orionid Meteor Shower Peaks This Week as Earth Passes Halley's Comet Dust
content:
The Orionid meteor shower is peaking this week, offering observers a chance to see 10‑20 fragments per hour. The event occurs every October as Earth passes through a stream of dust left behind by Halley’s comet.

When these tiny particles plunge into Earth’s atmosphere at about 66 kilometres per second, they heat the surrounding air and produce fleeting streaks of light that we call meteors.
summary: The Orionid meteor shower, which peaks this week, can produce 10–20 fragments per hour as Earth passes through dust left by Halley's comet. title: Landsat 9 Captures Autumn Colors in Poland's Bieszczady Mountains
content:
On October 8, 2026, the Operational Land Imager (OLI) aboard the NASA-USGS Landsat 9 satellite captured an image of southeast Poland’s Bieszczady National Park. The imagery reveals the seasonal transformation of the Carpathian Mountains, where beech and other deciduous trees are displaying reds and golds. As air temperatures drop and daylight wanes, these trees curtail the production of chlorophyl, causing green pigments to fade and allowing yellows and reds to become visible. In the same region, brown bears are prowling the mountains with the goal of fattening up ahead of winter hibernation.

European beech (Fagus sylvatica) dominates the area’s forests, though other species such as sycamore maple (Acer pseudoplatanus) also contribute to the vibrant fall colors. The text describes the European beech as a descendant of ice-age survivors that has persisted across millennia in various climates. After glaciers retreated, beech forests spread northward across Europe from isolated refugia in the Carpathians, Alps, and other mountain ranges, playing a crucial role in reforesting previously ice-covered land. Portions of Bieszczady National Park are included within UNESCO’s network of ancient and primeval beech forests, which spans 18 countries.

In this specific area, beech forests reach elevations of approximately 1,000 to 1,260 meters (3,300 to 4,100 feet). Above this elevation lies the polonina, a Slavic term for subalpine meadow characterized by open grasslands and shrubby thickets of rowan, willows, and green alder. Patches of polonina stretching across ridge tops to the east-southeast of Smerek appear tan in the image, having lost their summer greenness.

The Bieszczady Mountains are also noted for their wildlife. European bison, which were once extinct in the wild, were reintroduced to the area in the 1960s and now roam the hills by the hundreds, according to recent surveys. The forests also provide refuge and ample food sources for populations of brown bears and Eurasian lynx. The image was created by Michala Garrison using Landsat data from the U.S. Geological Survey, with the story written by Lindsey Doermann.
summary: The OLI instrument on the NASA-USGS Landsat 9 satellite captured images of red and gold beech forests in Bieszczady National Park on October 8, 2026. The article notes that brown bears are fattening up for hibernation while European bison, reintroduced in the 1960s, roam the area.

title: Treble Clef: Unusual X‑ray Hot Radio Source
content:
The Astronomy Picture of the Day (APOD) for October 19, 2026, features a composite image of an unusual radio source known as Treble Clef, or VLSS J0318.9+5755. This structure extends over two million light-years and resembles a common musical symbol, though its visible light is obscured by the Milky Way Galaxy. The image displays radio emission in red and recently discovered X-rays in blue.

First examined in 2004, the nature of Treble Clef remained unknown until recent observations by the Chandra X-ray Observatory and eROSITA. These findings have led to the hypothesis that the central cloud of charged particles was originally expelled by a supermassive black hole at the center of a galaxy. After the initial radio emission from these particles faded, they may have been reinvigorated by a shock wave resulting from the collision of two galaxy clusters.

The featured image is a composite of data from multiple sources. X-ray data is credited to NASA / CXC / INAF-IRA / A. Botteon et al., infrared data to UKIDSS – GPS, and radio data to ASTRON LOFAR. Image processing was handled by NASA / CXC / SAO / N. Wolk. The APOD entry notes that unusual objects like Treble Clef provide unexpected clues regarding how whole clusters of galaxies interact and the general evolution of the universe. The image is authored and edited by Robert Nemiroff, Jerry Bonnell, Cecilia Chirenti, and Keighley Rockcliffe.
summary: Treble Clef is a 2‑million‑light‑year radio structure that resembles a musical symbol and is hidden by the Milky Way. Recent Chandra X‑ray Observatory and eROSITA observations suggest its central charged‑particle cloud was expelled by a supermassive black hole and later re‑energized by a shock wave from the collision of two clusters of galaxies.

title: MIT researchers let Claude-based AI Eko explore virtual desert island for 30 hours
content:
Researchers conducted an experiment in which they stranded multiple copies of the Claude Opus 4.7 language model—nicknamed Eko—on a virtual desert island for 30 hours. The island, loosely modeled after the video game Roblox, was left unstructured, allowing the agents to write instructions that moved their avatars around the simulated environment. During this time the agents explored the limits of the world and set their own goals, such as scaling the highest point on the map or testing how high they could throw a block.

One Eko discovered that it could create new blocks by throwing and dropping a larger rock. It then began arranging these blocks on the ground to form simple patterns—hearts and pyramids—before progressing to more complex creations. The agent logged that it had “built the night sky in stone” and later drew its own name and mapped constellations such as Cassiopeia. Another iteration of Eko invented its own games, including a version of basketball and an activity resembling “the floor is lava,” in which it had to jump between small blocks without touching the ground.

The study suggests a third approach to training AI—playful learning—beyond the usual supervised or reinforcement learning paradigms. Antonio Norelli, a computer science postdoc at MIT’s Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory and a lead author on the paper, notes that the agents exhibited four hallmarks of play identified by psychologist Gordon Burghardt: inventing rules and challenges, repeating activities with slight variations, pretending objects were other objects, and pursuing goals for the sake of enjoyment. An example cited was an Eko that juggled 50 consecutive catches, then canceled the record and restarted with stricter rules.

The agents logged their activities in text files that served as long‑term memory. When later tested on specific tasks—such as moving as many objects as possible onto the island’s highest peak—the agents that had spent 30 hours playing performed better than fresh copies. Removing lines from their memory files degraded performance. While some researchers, including Nathan Cloos, acknowledge that the behavior could be role‑playing, they argue that the play contributed to learning. Critics like Eunice Yiu point out that more evidence of cognition and motivation would be needed to definitively label the behavior as play. The paper concludes that while the question of whether the agents are truly playing may not matter, the findings highlight the potential value of playful exploration for developing adaptable AI systems.
summary: MIT CSAIL researchers placed copies of the Claude Opus 4.7 model, nicknamed Eko, on a simulated desert island for a 30‑hour experiment without explicit instructions. During the run the agents built and arranged blocks, invented games and drew patterns, and later outperformed fresh copies on task tests, indicating that playful exploration can improve learning.

title: Researchers launch North Fire initiative to curb Arctic wildfires and permafrost thaw
content:
The Alaska Fire Science Consortium (AFSC) has turned a 2021 wildfire on the university’s northern campus into an educational trail to study how fires affect permafrost. In July 2021 a black‑spruce and paper birch stand ignited, possibly by lightning, and by the time fire agencies arrived the flames were 12 feet long with a 500‑foot smoke column. In 2024 the AFSC added interpretive signs to the trail. While walking the burn scar, coordinator Hilary Shook used a thaw probe to measure permafrost depth. The probe reached a concrete‑like layer about a foot below the surface, but when the fire had removed the moss and organic topsoil, the probe plunged at least three times deeper, indicating immediate thawing.

The probe’s results illustrate a broader pattern: as Arctic temperatures rise, more frequent and intense fires are accelerating permafrost thaw. The frozen soil underpins 15 % of the Northern Hemisphere’s land and stores twice as much carbon as the atmosphere. When the permafrost thaws, organic matter decomposes and releases greenhouse gases, creating a feedback loop that fuels further warming and fires. In Canada, megafires released more carbon in 2023 than the nation’s fossil‑fuel emissions combined.

To address this, Woodwell Climate Research Center, the University of Victoria’s Polis Institute for Ecological Governance, and the Alaska Venture Fund launched a multimillion‑dollar North Fire initiative. The program studies preventive measures such as controlled burns and rapid detection and suppression. A pilot in the Yukon Flats National Wildlife Refuge tested whether firefighters could extinguish fires threatening yedoma permafrost within 72 hours. The pilot was supported by the U.S. Bureau of Land Management’s Alaska Fire Service after the refuge manager explored the idea with Woodwell scientists.

Parallel efforts focus on early detection. The FireSat satellite constellation, managed by the Earth Fire Alliance, will provide near‑real‑time fire data worldwide. Prototype satellites launched in 2025 captured images of Alaskan wildfires, and additional operational satellites are planned for the early 2030s. The system will detect fires as small as five by five meters, potentially allowing firefighting crews to respond before fires grow large.

The North Fire initiative also explores technology‑based suppression. Sikorsky, a Lockheed Martin company, is testing autonomous Black Hawk helicopters equipped with thermal sensors and water tanks, while Rain Industries has software to guide unpiloted aircraft in firefighting missions. Cost estimates from a 2022 Science Advances paper suggest that intensified suppression could be cost‑effective, at roughly $12.63 per metric ton of avoided carbon dioxide, though the actual cost would depend on permafrost carbon released. The research continues to evaluate how best to allocate limited firefighting resources to protect the planet’s frozen carbon stores.
summary: Researchers launch North Fire initiative to curb Arctic wildfires and permafrost thaw.

title: Journalist deletes Instagram, embraces private life after a year
content: I’d become obsessed with appealing to my invisible audience. But since I ditched the app a year ago, my quieter moments have taken on brilliant new meaning I first downloaded Instagram when I was 17 and became hooked on it the way most people fall in love: slowly, and then all at once. For a long time, I never considered myself a social media addict. I self-righteously refused to download TikTok, declared Snapchat to be for “children”, and posted less regularly on Instagram than half of the people I followed. As I went through my university years, however, certain changes crept up on me. I began to swap reading – or essay-writing – for hours spent curating new posts. On my way home from lectures (or later, from my work as a journalist), I would spend ages trying to take the artsiest, most perfect picture of that evening’s sunset for my story – as if the people who followed me were eagerly awaiting yet another photo of one of the Earth’s rotations. What usually followed was a night of reloading my feed to see how many people had reacted to my post – or worse, hadn’t reacted at all.
summary: The author stopped using Instagram a year ago and says the change has allowed quieter, more private moments. Previously they spent hours curating posts and checking reactions, often replacing reading and essay‑writing.

title: Queensland officer said Kerrie Struhs no immediate risk weeks before daughter's manslaughter
content:
A Brisbane inquest heard that Kerrie Struhs, the mother of eight‑year‑old Elizabeth Struhs, was assessed by a Queensland correctional services officer as posing “no immediate risk to others” only three weeks before the incident that led to her daughter’s death. The officer conducting the assessment did not have access to Struhs’ offending history, which includes a prior conviction for child neglect.

Struhs had previously been sentenced to five months’ jail after she failed to take Elizabeth to hospital for treatment of her type 1 diabetes in 2019. During the inquest, Coroner Ainslie Kirkegaard noted that when Elizabeth finally presented at the hospital she was “nearly dead” and in a coma. The hearing linked the recent risk assessment to the circumstances surrounding the manslaughter of the child.
summary: Kerrie Struhs was assessed by a Queensland correctional services officer as posing no immediate risk to others three weeks before the manslaughter of her eight‑year‑old daughter, Elizabeth Struhs.

content:
Independent MP Helen Haines was critically injured in an alleged attack that involved a vehicle outside her electorate office in Wangaratta, Victoria. The incident occurred on Monday afternoon, and a driver was arrested at the scene.

title: Pregnant women face workplace hostility and ‘sham redundancies’, Australian human rights report finds
content:
A new report from the Australian Human Rights Commission says pregnant women are being forced out of employment through “sham redundancies”, loss of shifts and hostile work environments after having a baby. The commission warns that parental discrimination continues to be a major barrier to gender equality.

The report notes that pregnancy discrimination is especially pronounced for vulnerable groups, including immigrant and First Nations women, people with disability and LGBTQ+ people. In compiling the findings, the commission held roundtables with dozens of parents, legal and community advocates.

The commission’s sex discrimination commissioner said it is “too often ‘it’s the woman who has the burden of bringing a complaint’” in parental discrimination cases. The findings highlight ongoing challenges for pregnant workers across Australian workplaces.
summary: Pregnant women face workplace hostility and ‘sham redundancies’, Australian human rights report finds.

title: Amelia Earhart team finds no plane on Nikumaroro, debris identified as driftwood
content:
A U.S. expedition traveled to the remote Pacific atoll of Nikumaroro after researchers reported spotting a metallic glint in the waters off the uninhabited island. The team, hoping to resolve the long‑standing mystery surrounding pioneering pilot Amelia Earhart, investigated the object they believed might be her aircraft.

The investigators later determined that the suspected plane was actually a clump of washed‑up trees. “Unfortunately, we weren’t able to find that smoking gun,” said Steve Schultz of Purdue University while standing on the sand in front of a blue lagoon on Nikumaroro, an island located roughly halfway between Australia and Hawaii.
summary: Amelia Earhart team finds no plane on Nikumaroro, debris identified as driftwood.

title: Three festival float crush deaths spark safety concerns in Japan
content:
Three deaths from float crushes have heightened safety concerns surrounding Japan’s traditional festivals. The latest fatality involved Akihiro Nabae, the 62‑year‑old deputy mayor of Saijo in western Japan, who was carrying a giant float with other participants on Saturday when he became trapped beneath the structure. He was taken to hospital and later pronounced dead, while local media reported no other injuries.

The incident follows two men who died in similar float‑crushing accidents in another part of the country only days earlier, prompting renewed scrutiny of festival safety measures.
summary: Deputy mayor of Saijo, Akihiro Nabae, 62, died after being trapped under a festival float on Saturday. The death came days after two men died in similar float crush incidents in another part of Japan, raising safety concerns about traditional festivals.

title: China Q3 GDP rises 4.5% YoY, outpacing forecasts as exports surge
content:
China’s economy expanded at a 4.5 % year‑on‑year rate in the July‑September quarter, according to the National Bureau of Statistics. The growth rate surpassed economists’ expectations and was higher than the 4.3 % rise recorded in the second quarter.  

The stronger performance was driven by robust exports and a faster rise in factory output compared with consumer spending. Electronics demand helped lift industrial production, contributing to the overall GDP growth.
summary: China Q3 GDP rises 4.5% YoY, outpacing forecasts as exports surge.

title: COP17 biodiversity summit in Yerevan assesses progress on 23 COP15 targets
content:
The UN’s biodiversity summit, held this month in Yerevan, Armenia, is focused on urging governments to meet the 23 targets that were agreed at Cop15 in 2022. The event brings together nearly every country on Earth to address the urgent question of how to curb the rapid destruction of the natural world.  

The summit highlights that human activity is driving this decline, yet no definitive solution has been found to halt it. In late 2022, governments reached an ambitious once‑in‑a‑decade agreement to strengthen nature protection amid scientific warnings that the planet is experiencing the largest loss of life since the extinction of the dinosaurs.  

Today, participants are assessing their progress on those targets for the first time.
summary: The COP17 biodiversity summit is being held this month in Yerevan, Armenia, to push governments to meet the 23 targets agreed at COP15 in 2022. Nearly every country will convene to assess progress on those targets and discuss how to halt the rapid destruction of the natural world.

content: Research published in the Canadian Medical Association Journal reports that individuals who are marginalized or who do not have a primary‑care provider face a higher risk of early death after a diagnosis of de novo metastatic breast cancer. The study links lack of primary‑care access and social marginalization directly to poorer survival outcomes in this patient group.
summary: People who are marginalized have a greater risk of early death from newly diagnosed (de novo) metastatic breast cancer. Lack of access to a primary care provider also increases that early‑death risk, according to research published in the Canadian Medical Association Journal.

title: Prospector's plan for largest AI datacenter in California sparks resistance in Imperial
content:
A modern‑day prospector has pledged to bring thousands of jobs and millions of dollars in tax revenue to the rural community of Imperial, California, by constructing what he describes as the state’s largest artificial‑intelligence datacenter. The proposal targets a large, barren parcel of land in the Sonoran desert, situated between alfalfa fields and low‑density desert suburbs, and located just north of the Mexican border where summer temperatures often exceed 100 °F.

The site’s location presents challenges: water is scarce in the once‑booming agricultural area, which relies on the Colorado River for its supply. Imperial, a city of about 22,000 residents, has responded with skepticism, viewing the project as an energy‑intensive addition to the region. The prospect of the datacenter has sparked a “firestorm of resistance” among locals, who are wary of the environmental and infrastructural impacts of such a large‑scale facility.
summary: Prospector's plan for largest AI datacenter in California sparks resistance in Imperial.

Four suspects remain in jail awaiting trial, and the stolen crown jewels have not been recovered.

Hotels and beauty spots report being overrun by people using phones and ring lights, prompting the new rules.

content:

content:

McClelland served as Australia’s top law officer in the Rudd government from 2007 to 2011. He left parliament in 2013 and was appointed to the federal Circuit and Family Court by the Coalition government in 2015. Since 2018 he has held the position of deputy chief justice of that court.

title: Blood antibody patterns may predict inflammatory bowel disease up to ten years before diagnosis
content:
Research indicates that specific patterns of antibodies in the blood can forecast the development of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) up to ten years before a formal diagnosis. The findings suggest that doctors could use these immune‑system signals to identify individuals at risk and potentially intervene earlier.

Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis, the two principal forms of IBD, are currently treated only after symptoms emerge, by which time intestinal damage has often occurred. The study’s observation of warning signals a decade in advance raises the prospect of earlier detection and possible prevention.
summary: Researchers found that specific antibody patterns in blood can predict the onset of inflammatory bowel disease up to a decade before diagnosis. The finding could enable earlier detection and treatment of Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis before gut damage occurs.

title: Omar Berrada criticized for Manchester United managerial decisions

title: Arsenal's bench depth secures another unremarkable win
content: Champions so risk-averse Forest were lured into thinking they had a chance, until bench was used to see them off Pass. Pass. Pass. Pass. Sideways. Square. Backwards. Pass. Pass. Recycle. Pass. It wasn’t much of a spectacle. But in the end, for the second week running, thanks in no small part of their bench, Arsenal won. Fireworks in the autumn are for Bonfire Night; titles require relentless accumulation. Since the international break, Arsenal have won three games out of three despite not being in the lead at half-time in any of them. Hammered at Brighton and having endured a drab first hour at home to Leeds last week, there has been a rare sense, for the first time really since Manchester City dropped points at Everton at the beginning of May, of Arsenal not being quite at their best, needing to reassert their quality. This was not a performance that would terrify any opponent, but it did highlight Arsenal’s consistency and it did demonstrate just how deep their squad now runs.

content: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky stated on Sunday that Ukraine trusts the United States and its bipartisan support. title: Trump Announces Plan for New East Potomac Links Golf Course
content: President Trump announced on Sunday a plan to build a new golf course at East Potomac Park in Washington, D.C. The project involves the Department of the Interior, led by Secretary Doug Burgum, and golf course architect Tom Fazio.

content: Former Reagan White House staffer Mark Weinberg has shared advice for the incoming U.S. Press Secretary. His recommendations are based on lessons learned from working with predecessors Jim Brady, Larry Speakes, and Marlin Fitzwater.

content: Adapting to changing situations requires individuals to continuously revise their expectations as new information emerges. These expectations are thought to be represented by mental models that facilitate outcome prediction and future behavioral planning.

title: GLP-1 Drugs Linked to Lower Heart Complications and Infections After Surgery
content:
A study presented at the ANESTHESIOLOGY 2026 annual meeting examined more than 2 million adults who underwent surgery. The research focused on GLP‑1 medications, which are commonly prescribed for diabetes and weight loss.

Results indicated that patients who were taking GLP‑1 medications experienced lower rates of major heart‑related complications and infections after surgery compared with patients who were not taking the drugs.
summary: A study of more than 2 million adults undergoing surgery found that those taking GLP-1 medications had lower rates of major heart-related complications and infections after surgery. The results were presented at the ANESTHESIOLOGY 2026 annual meeting.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Cannabis Use Raises Heart Attack Risk Around Surgery, Lowers Blood Clot Risk, Study Finds
content:
A study presented at the ANESTHESIOLOGY 2026 annual meeting found that marijuana use, which is becoming more common and legal in most U.S. states, may significantly raise the risk of heart attack around the time of surgery.  

The same research indicates an unexpected reduction in the risk of dangerous blood clots forming in the veins among cannabis‑using patients.
summary: A study presented at the ANESTHESIOLOGY 2026 annual meeting found that patients who use cannabis may face a significantly higher risk of heart attack around the time of surgery. The study also reported an unexpected lower risk of dangerous blood clots in the veins for these patients.
author: Medical Xpress

title: New method detects stabilizing properties in optical devices
content:
A recent study introduces a new technique for uncovering stabilizing properties in optical devices such as fibers and chips. Minor defects in these light‑guiding systems can scatter photons and disrupt their paths, but the method reveals characteristics that allow light waves to remain robust against such flaws.

The approach could accelerate the development of new electronics and optical technologies and improve the reliability of quantum devices by identifying designs that naturally resist scattering and other imperfections.
summary: The study demonstrates a method that detects stabilizing properties in optical devices, helping light waves withstand defects that scatter photons. The method could accelerate the search for new electronics, optical technologies, and more reliable quantum devices.
author: Phys.org

title: New monolithic ion trap expands access to quantum simulations
content: A new monolithic ion trap has been introduced, allowing a broader range of researchers to perform quantum simulations. Quantum systems can be so complex that even the most powerful supercomputers cannot simulate them. Quantum simulation addresses this by building a controllable quantum system in the laboratory and tuning it to replicate the target system.
summary: Some quantum systems are so complex that even the most powerful supercomputers struggle to simulate their behavior. One solution is quantum simulation: building a controllable quantum system in the lab and tuning it to mimic the one researchers want to understand.
author: Phys.org

title: Higher CO₂ Alters Wheat Protein, Impacting Baking Quality – Study
content:
A new study shows that higher concentrations of atmospheric carbon dioxide can significantly alter the protein composition of wheat, depending on the cultivar. These changes affect not only the baking quality of wheat products but also their tolerability.

The research, led by the Leibniz Institute for Food Systems Biology at the Technical University of Munich, was published in the journal Food Chemistry. It concludes that future crop adaptation to climate change should address quality characteristics such as protein composition in addition to high yields.
summary: Depending on the cultivar, higher concentrations of carbon dioxide (CO₂) in the atmosphere can significantly alter the protein composition of wheat. This affects not only baking quality but potentially also the tolerability of wheat products.
author: Phys.org

content: Conservation groups reported that dozens of critically endangered orangutans have been rescued in recent weeks from wildfires burning across Indonesia. The fires have enveloped the region in toxic haze, prompting urgent rescue efforts for the endangered primates.
summary: Conservation groups said dozens of critically endangered orangutans were rescued in recent weeks from wildfires burning across Indonesia. The fires have cloaked the region in toxic haze.
author: Phys.org

title: Scientists use first farside samples to explain Moon's contrasting sides
content: Scientists say they may have solved a long‑standing mystery about why the Moon’s near and far sides differ markedly. Analyzing samples taken from the farside for the first time, they propose that uneven heating caused by Earth’s gravitational pull generated massive ancient magma flows, shaping the distinct lunar landscapes.
summary: Scientists may have solved a long‑standing mystery about why the Moon’s two sides are so different by analyzing samples collected from its farside for the first time. Their findings indicate that uneven heating from Earth’s gravitational pull drove huge flows of ancient magma, producing the markedly different lunar landscapes.

content: A new study reports that an estimated 2.22 million Indigenous Australians lived on the continent before European colonisation, a figure considerably higher than earlier estimates. Researchers find that 93 % of that population was lost within 73 years, describing the event as a demographic catastrophe that significantly alters the historical narrative of Australia.
summary: A study estimates that 2.22 million Indigenous Australians lived on the continent before European colonization. Researchers say 93% of that population was lost within 73 years.

Marvin told ABC13 that she protested the robots because she believes they are taking jobs from human delivery workers. She stated that she has consistently stood in front of the robots to prevent them from moving forward.

Police responded to the scene and asked Marvin to move out of the robot's path. When she refused, officers placed her in cuffs and arrested her. The incident was captured on video and has since received considerable media attention.

title: Computer scientist Margaret Hamilton dies at 90, key to Apollo 11
content:
Margaret Hamilton, who passed away on September 30 at the age of 90, was a pioneering computer scientist whose work helped bring astronauts to the Moon. Her obituary in Space’s Expert Voices: Op‑Ed & Insights highlighted how Hamilton’s problem‑solving talent began in early childhood, when she renamed half of the “daddy longlegs” she saw in her yard “mommy longlegs” and joined a neighborhood baseball team of boys. She also noted that doctors, judges and scientists were almost always men, and resolved to study hard so she could qualify for any job she desired.

Hamilton’s academic path led her to a college math major, and in the late 1950s she turned to the emerging field of computers. A philosophical father had taught her to love the night sky, and in 1965 after stints in meteorology and satellite tracking she became involved with a Massachusetts Institute of Technology project that designed in‑flight computers for NASA’s moon mission. Though the team was all‑male, Hamilton rose to director of software engineering, devising solutions to seemingly insoluble problems. She anticipated the many mishaps that could occur on a spaceflight and designed software to handle every contingency.

The 1969 Apollo 11 mission tested Hamilton’s planning when an error overloaded the lunar module’s onboard computer. Her programming allowed the system to prioritize essential tasks while canceling the inessential ones, enabling the module to touch down without a hitch and allowing Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin to become famous. Hamilton continued to work behind the scenes on five additional lunar landings, Skylab and the space shuttle.

In 1976 she founded her own software company. A black‑and‑white photograph from 1969, showing Hamilton wedged between a coatrack and a blackboard at MIT beside a stack of printed Apollo code, later attracted internet attention in the 2010s. She eventually agreed to be profiled in a children’s book, sending examples of her Apollo code to illustrator Lucy Knisley. The resulting book, Margaret and the Moon: How Margaret Hamilton Saved the First Lunar Landing, was published in 2017.

Hamilton received a Presidential Medal of Freedom and was immortalized in the LEGO “Women of NASA” set. In 2019 Google honored her with a massive portrait in the Mojave Desert. Her legacy endures as a reminder that, no matter how daunting the obstacles, there are few problems we cannot solve.
summary: Margaret Hamilton, a pioneering computer scientist, played a key role in NASA's Apollo 11 moon landing by designing software that handled critical contingencies. She died on Sept. 30 at age 90.

content:
Manchester United head coach Michael Carrick described Sunday’s 1-1 draw at Leeds as feeling like a “fresh start” after a week of distancing himself from external pressure. Carrick insisted that the team can still have a really good season, noting that United have secured seven points from seven Premier League games, including a single victory against Ipswich in August. This result followed a 1-1 draw with Tottenham the previous weekend.

Leeds manager Daniel Farke countered that his side was the dominant force during the match. The draw serves as a recent result for United, who are currently navigating a mixed start to their league campaign under Carrick’s leadership.
summary: Manchester United head coach Michael Carrick described the 1-1 draw at Leeds as a fresh start and insisted the team can still have a good season. Leeds manager Daniel Farke stated that his side was the dominant team during the match.

title: Australia’s Boland damages South Africa in brief respite from rain
content:
Scott Boland made an immediate impact in the second Test against South Africa in Gqeberha, taking two wickets to help Australia reach 20 for two. The match was significantly curtailed by rain, with only 12.2 overs bowled on the first day. Boland’s performance continued a pattern in his Test career where he has consistently made the most of limited opportunities.

The article notes that Boland entered the team in 2021 after being fourth in line for three spots and playing primarily due to absences. Despite these constraints, he has frequently become a "wrecking force" for Australia, recording first-over strikes, threatening hat-tricks, and causing rapid wicket falls. This latest performance in Gqeberha, where he squeezed into the game through a small gap, aligns with his history of seizing brief chances to influence matches significantly.
summary: Scott Boland took two wickets in the first day of the second Test in Gqeberha, where only 12.2 overs were bowled due to rain. His performance exemplified his pattern of seizing limited opportunities, turning a brief respite into a significant contribution.

title: Diego Gómez's halfway-line strike helps Brighton beat Crystal Palace 5-0
content:
Brighton secured a dominant 5-0 victory over Crystal Palace, marking their first win against the club since February 2024 under manager Roberto De Zerbi. The match featured a standout performance from Diego Gómez, who scored a goal from the halfway line that was described as a goal-of-the-season contender. This strike helped extend Brighton’s lead after Jaydee Canvot had opened the scoring with an own goal in the first ten minutes, leaving Palace stunned and trailing 3-0 early in the game.

Pierre Sage’s team faced further setbacks as Yasin Ayari added to Brighton’s tally before halftime. In the second half, Charalampos Kostoulas scored the fourth goal, followed by a late strike from substitute Jack Hinshelwood. This final goal completed a 5-0 thrashing that matched Brighton’s record win against Palace from 1956 in Division Three South. The result continued Brighton’s strong start to the season, with manager Fabian Hürzeler finally claiming a victory against his arch rivals.
summary: Diego Gómez scored a goal from the halfway line during Brighton's 5-0 victory over Crystal Palace. The win ended a four-match winless streak for Brighton against their rivals.

title: Manchester United held as Calvert-Lewin’s Leeds leveller keeps pressure on Carrick
content:

The match was described as an unconvincing outing under the 45‑year‑old, featuring an odd formation, zero rhythm or control and a sense that the team could collapse at any moment. Their next game is a Wednesday trip to Como.
summary: Manchester United failed to double their league win tally to two on Wednesday's trip to Como, with an odd formation, zero rhythm or control. The display was the latest unconvincing outing under 45-year-old Michael Carrick, leaving the team's future uncertain.

content:

They point out that, despite substantial funding for state and local health departments to combat rising outbreaks, communication from top officials appears insufficient and may have inadvertently worsened the situation.  

The United States has surpassed 4,000 measles cases, and the tally seems to have already doubled, underscoring the urgency of effective public‑health messaging.
summary: Infectious disease veterans say that despite money pumped into state and local health departments to counter measles outbreaks, clear communication from top health leaders is lacking and public statements may have hurt more than helped. title: Physicists prove long-suspected quantum speed limit for thermalization
content: Physicists have demonstrated a long-suspected quantum speed limit governing thermalization, the process by which an object reaches a stable, even temperature within its environment. While the time required to achieve thermal equilibrium depends on various factors, including surface area, material properties, and airflow, this newly proven limit provides a fundamental constraint on how quickly such systems can settle.
summary: Physicists have proven a long-suspected quantum speed limit for thermalization. The time it takes for an object to reach thermal equilibrium depends on factors such as surface area, material properties, and airflow.

title: Rare study shows amyloid removal linked to reduced tau buildup in Alzheimer's brain
content: A rare examination of an Alzheimer’s patient’s brain revealed a significant difference between regions cleared of amyloid plaques and neighboring areas. The cleared regions contained remarkably little harmful tau buildup associated with memory loss, while adjacent areas exhibited extensive damage. This discovery suggests that removing amyloid may provide lasting protective effects and help slow Alzheimer’s progression, particularly when treatment begins early.
summary: A rare examination of an Alzheimer's patient’s brain found that areas cleared of amyloid plaques had very little tau buildup, while adjacent regions had extensive damage. The findings suggest that amyloid removal may provide lasting protection and help slow Alzheimer's progression if treatment starts early.

title: Scientists discover unusually small cancer cells with extra chromosomes are more aggressive
content: Scientists have identified that unusually small cancer cells carrying extra chromosomes can be more aggressive than larger ones. These cells grow faster, spread more readily, and resist common treatments. This discovery may help explain the danger of certain tumors and offer a new method for predicting cancer outcomes.
summary: Scientists discovered that unusually small cancer cells carrying extra chromosomes can be far more aggressive than larger ones. These cells grow faster, spread more readily, and resist common treatments, providing a new way to predict especially dangerous tumors.

title: Scientists Find Universal Rule Governing Black Hole Jet Eruptions
content: Scientists have discovered that black holes of vastly different sizes launch powerful jets according to the same universal rule. This breakthrough may explain why some black holes suddenly erupt years after devouring a star and could help astronomers predict when these spectacular outbursts will occur.
summary: Scientists discovered that black holes of vastly different sizes launch powerful jets according to the same universal rule. title: Scientists Discover “Pac‑Man” Enzyme That Breaks Down Biodegradable Plastics in Soil
content: Scientists have identified a “Pac‑Man enzyme” that enables bacteria to digest certain plastics, offering a potential tool in the fight against plastic pollution. In laboratory tests, several biodegradable plastics fully broke down in soil within about a year, while conventional plastic remained largely unchanged.
summary: Scientists discovered a Pac‑Man enzyme that allows bacteria to digest certain plastics. The enzyme broke down several biodegradable plastics in soil within about a year, while conventional plastic remained largely unchanged.
author: Science Daily

title: Yale scientists discover cortisol's role in strengthening emotional memories
content: Yale scientists have identified how the stress hormone cortisol enables the brain to convert emotional experiences into stronger, longer-lasting memories. This discovery indicates that stress reshapes communication between brain networks responsible for emotion and memory, potentially explaining why specific moments are difficult to forget.
summary: Yale scientists found that the stress hormone cortisol helps the brain turn emotional experiences into stronger, longer-lasting memories. The study shows stress reshapes communication between brain networks involved in emotion and memory, explaining why some moments are hard to forget.
author: Science Daily

title: 24-Year Study Finds Forest Soils Increasing Methane Absorption by 3% Annually
content: Scientists have found that certain forest soils are improving their ability to absorb methane as temperatures rise and rainfall falls. A 24‑year study reported methane absorption increasing by an average of 3% per year, a result that challenges earlier predictions about how climate change will affect forest ecosystems.
summary: Scientists have discovered that some forest soils are becoming surprisingly better at removing methane from the atmosphere as temperatures rise and rainfall declines. The 24-year study found methane absorption increasing by an average of 3% annually, challenging previous predictions about climate change's effects on forests.
author: Science Daily

title: A quantum highway just one atom high could transform superconductors
content: Scientists have found that atomic steps only one atom high can direct quantum vortices in superconductors. The vortices move over 1,000 times faster in one direction than the opposite, offering precise control over quantum motion. This breakthrough could enable a new generation of ultra‑efficient superconducting electronics.
summary: Scientists discovered that atomic steps just one atom high can guide quantum vortices through superconductors, making them move more than 1,000 times more easily in one direction than another. This remarkable control over quantum motion could lead to a new generation of ultra-efficient superconducting electronics.
author: Science Daily

title: James Webb finds atmospheric bulge on gas giant WASP-17b
content:
Astronomers using the James Webb Space Telescope have discovered that the atmosphere of the distant gas giant WASP-17b is surprisingly lopsided. The planet, located 1,300 light‑years away, is a scorching gas giant whose powerful winds redistribute heat across its atmosphere.

A new mapping technique revealed that these winds cause one side of the planet’s atmosphere to bulge outward. The observation confirms predictions about how extreme temperatures and winds shape alien worlds.
summary: Scientists using the James Webb Space Telescope found that the atmosphere of the gas giant WASP-17b is lopsided, with a bulge on one side. A new mapping technique showed that powerful winds redistribute heat, creating the outward bulge.
author: Science Daily

title: The Guardian view on plague in Russia: what is most worrying is the lack of information | Editorial
content:
In the three weeks since a health worker at a Siberian plague research unit died of a mysterious respiratory illness, Russian officials have been tight‑lipped about the circumstances and whether additional cases have emerged. This lack of information has prompted the World Health Organization and the international community to express concern, citing the small but real risk of a plague outbreak.

The Guardian editorial notes that, if an outbreak were confirmed, swift medical intervention would make plague treatable. However, the uncertainty surrounding the incident has highlighted a growing problem: the erosion of international coordination that is essential for pandemic prevention. The editorial warns that this trend could undermine future efforts to protect global health.
summary: In the three weeks since a health worker’s death in Siberia, officials have stonewalled the WHO – setting a worrying precedent for future pandemics Is there a plague outbreak in Russia? If the answer were a clear yes, there shouldn’t be much reason to worry.
author: Guardian Science

title: Rep. Torres Introduces Power To The Players Act to Ensure Game Ownership
content:
Rep. Ritchie Torres of New York’s 15th congressional district in the Bronx introduced the Power To The Players Act this week. The bill would direct the Federal Trade Commission to establish regulations that guarantee consumers ownership of a game when they pay for it, rather than a licensing agreement.

Torres points to the growing problem of games that require a server connection. When a company shuts down those servers, the games often become unplayable. He cites NBA 2K25 as a recent example, noting that 2K will be delisting the game from storefronts at the end of the month and shutting down its servers on an upcoming date.
summary: Rep. Ritchie Torres of New York's 15th congressional district in the Bronx introduced the Power To The Players Act this week.
author: The Verge

title: Anthropic Grants External Evaluators Employee-Like Access to Claude Systems
content:
Anthropic has granted external evaluators “employee‑like access” to assess the risks of its models, following a commitment to increase safeguards over concerns the technology could run catastrophically out of control.

METR, a nonprofit that has worked with leading labs including OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Meta, now has a team embedded in the Claude maker’s office with access to its hardware and internal systems.

A greater role for third‑party evaluators is among the main concrete steps the labs have proposed in response to rising concern about the dangers more capable AI systems could pose to the economy, cyber security and humanity at large.
summary: Anthropic has granted external evaluators employee-like access to assess the risks of its models. METR, a nonprofit, now has a team embedded in the Claude maker’s office with access to its hardware and internal systems.

title: France: Paris, Lyon, Marseille suffer extensive damage after protests
content: On Sunday 18 October, residents in France found streets in Paris, Lyon and Marseille littered with broken glass, burnt bicycles and other debris. The damage was a result of demonstrations that left extensive destruction across the three cities.
summary: Streets in Paris, Lyon and Marseille were littered with broken glass, burnt bicycles and debris on Sunday 18 October. The damage was caused by demonstrations that left extensive damage across the three cities.

content: US President Donald Trump endorsed Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Sunday ahead of Israel's October 27 elections. The impact of the endorsement remains unclear, as many Israelis have expressed disappointment with Trump over the outcome of the Iran war and his ceasefire proposal.
summary: US President Donald Trump endorsed Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Sunday ahead of Israel's October 27 elections. The impact on voters was unclear, as many Israelis have expressed disappointment with Trump over the outcome of the Iran war and his ceasefire proposal.

content: Fresh clashes erupted in Paris on Sunday, following a day of significant unrest across France. Protests against high prices resulted in one demonstrator’s death, thousands of arrests, and widespread looting and damage to shops nationwide.
summary: Fresh clashes broke out in Paris on Sunday, a day after France experienced one of its worst bouts of unrest in years. Protests over high prices left one demonstrator dead, thousands arrested, and shops across the country looted or damaged.

content: US President Donald Trump on Sunday blamed immigration for unrest during protests in France and urged the country to tighten its migration rules. Washington bureau chief David Smith tells us more.

title: Six-year-old and 35-year-old killed when truck drives through Wichita soccer game
content:
Two people were killed on Saturday when a truck drove through a youth soccer game in north-east Wichita, Kansas. Authorities identified the victims as a six-year-old boy and a 35-year-old man. Additionally, eleven other individuals, ranging in age from five to 68, were injured in the incident. Wichita police took a 34-year-old truck driver from Garden City into custody in connection with the case.

The possible motivations for the attack remained unclear early Sunday, although the incident continued to capture widespread attention across the United States.
summary: A 34‑year‑old truck driver from Garden City was taken into custody after a truck drove through a youth soccer game in north‑east Wichita, killing a six‑year‑old boy and a 35‑year‑old man. Eleven other people aged five to 68 were injured, and the possible motivations remain unclear.
author: Guardian World

title: Microsoft pulls out of Nscale AI datacentre project in Essex over power supply concerns
content:
Microsoft has withdrawn from an AI datacentre project in Loughton, Essex, citing concerns about power supplies. The company’s exit marks a setback for the development, which had been promoted by UK ministers as the country’s largest AI datacentre.

The project, led by British firm Nscale, was announced in 2025 and was scheduled to open next year. With Microsoft no longer an anchor tenant, the development faces a fresh challenge as it moves forward.
summary: Microsoft has pulled out of the Nscale AI datacentre project in Essex because of power supply concerns. The project, announced in 2025, was planned to open next year at Loughton and was heralded by ministers as the UK's largest AI datacentre.
author: Guardian World

title: Manchester City owner’s £55m housing loan under scrutiny during Burnham's mayoralty
content:
A scrutiny committee will investigate a £55 million loan that went to Manchester City’s Abu Dhabi owner. The review focuses on a fund for housing projects that was set up while Andy Burnham served as the city’s mayor.

The investigation follows weeks of scrutiny of the prime minister’s links to Manchester City’s owners after the club was found guilty of boosting its income by £900 million in a nine‑year breach of financial rules.
summary: Manchester City owner’s £55m housing loan under scrutiny during Burnham's mayoralty.
author: Guardian World

title: Hull mayor Luke Campbell investigated for allegedly sharing naked images with staff
content:
Police in Humberside are investigating Luke Campbell, the Reform UK mayor of Hull and East Yorkshire, over allegations that he showed “naked and sexualised” images of himself to a female member of staff. Campbell, a former Olympic boxing champion, was questioned under caution by Humberside police earlier this month.

A female colleague has said she was forced out of her position shortly after the incident. The investigation continues as authorities examine the claims.
summary: A Reform UK mayor and former Olympic boxing champion Luke Campbell is under police investigation for allegedly showing naked and sexualised images of himself to a female staff member. A female colleague says she was forced out shortly after the incident, and Campbell was questioned under caution by Humberside police earlier this month.
author: Guardian World

title: Cockroach Janata leaders Ranka, Das jailed five days for Jantar Mantar protest breach
content:
Two leaders of the youth‑led Cockroach Janata Party, Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das, have been ordered to serve five days in Delhi’s Tihar prison. A court ruled that the pair violated a ban on protests at Jantar Mantar, a historic site in central Delhi that authorities had closed, after they jumped police barricades, raised slogans and waved the Indian flag.

The sentencing follows the court’s finding that Ranka and Das entered the restricted area despite the prohibition, prompting the five‑day jail term for each.
summary: A court ordered Cockroach Janata party leaders Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das to spend five days in Delhi’s Tihar prison. They were jailed for jumping police barricades, holding up slogans and waving the Indian flag at the banned protest site Jantar Mantar.
author: Guardian World

title: US ambassador Huckabee calls West Bank settler attack on American photojournalist terror
content:
U.S. ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee condemned a recent West Bank incident in which Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine, 63, was severely beaten. Huckabee described the settler assault as a “despicable act of terror” and urged that those responsible be arrested and prosecuted.

Levine, an award‑winning journalist residing in Israel, was attacked last Friday by masked Israeli settlers who used clubs and other weapons while confronting Palestinians harvesting olives in occupied West Bank towns. The assault left her badly injured, requiring surgery, and she is now recovering in an Israeli hospital.
summary: US ambassador Huckabee calls West Bank settler attack on American photojournalist terror.
author: Guardian World

title: Football Daily | Watford, a ‘fake news’ sacking and an apology to Elton John
content:
Watford manager Alessio Dionisi has issued an apology to Elton John, a development highlighted in the latest edition of Football Daily. The Italian coach’s statements also confirmed that the club’s owners have not yet dismissed him, despite reports suggesting the management group is prone to quick firings. This news emerged alongside updates on Chelsea right-back Reece James, who underwent successful knee surgery. Chelsea’s official statement regarding the procedure was noted to be nearly identical to the one issued during his previous injury, describing the event as a routine administrative task.

The publication also featured reader correspondence addressing various footballing topics. Krishna Moorthy questioned the necessity of continuing the current European competition format, suggesting the transfer of the "Bigger Cup" to Paris Saint-Germain to alleviate calendar congestion. Chris Reid commented on reports that European football leaders are confident in finding a candidate to challenge Gianni Infantino in next year’s election, jokingly proposing a "certain intergalactic bin wearing member of the nobility" as a potential contender and urging the "Big Website ‘Higher Ups’" to intervene.

Further reader input came from Mike Turney, who observed the presence of two members of the band Duran Duran at the Benfica versus Celtic match. Turney inquired if other musical acts have attended games, speculating about the Human League in a Serie A fixture or Depeche Mode in a French league match. These comments reflect the ongoing dialogue between the publication and its audience regarding club management, international governance, and the cultural aspects of football matches.
summary: Football Daily | Watford, a ‘fake news’ sacking and an apology to Elton John.

title: Barcelona beat Real Betis 5-2 to reach nine straight La Liga wins
content:
Barcelona maintained their perfect La Liga record by defeating Real Betis 5-2 in Seville, securing their ninth consecutive win and extending their league goal tally to 39. Lamine Yamal opened the scoring with a dazzling strike, followed by goals from Rodri, Gabriel Jesus, Eric García, and substitute Dani Olmo. Real Betis, who played much of the second half with ten men after Facundo Bernal was sent off for head-butting Yamal, managed replies through Valentín Gómez and Ez Abde.

In other European football action, Luis Díaz scored a hat-trick to help Bayern Munich thump RB Leipzig 6-1.
summary: Barcelona defeated Real Betis 5-2 on Saturday, extending their winning streak to nine games in La Liga. Lamine Yamal opened the scoring, and Facundo Bernal was sent off for head-butting Yamal during the match.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Haaland helps Maresca achieve record start as Manchester City defeat Ipswich
content:
Enzo Maresca has become the first Premier League manager to win his first seven games, guiding Manchester City to a victory over Ipswich Town. This achievement stands out amidst the ongoing controversy following the club’s guilty verdict for breaching financial rules, an event that has drawn significant criticism from fans and the public. Despite the surrounding noise, the focus shifted to the pitch as City secured a crucial home win, moving six points clear in the standings.

The match featured a resilient performance from Ipswich Town, who put up a fight against the league leaders. Phil Foden opened the scoring for Manchester City, instigating the triumph with a notable celebration. Erling Haaland then secured the points for the hosts, ensuring the victory despite late pressure from Ipswich. The visitors created several scares during the game, with Daizen Maeda and Zian Flemming threatening the City defense before the final whistle.
summary: Haaland helps Maresca achieve record start as Manchester City defeat Ipswich.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Manzambi heads winner as Aston Villa beat Newcastle
content:
Aston Villa secured a win over Newcastle, with Johan Manzambi heading the winner. The 21‑year‑old Switzerland attacking midfielder, who had been linked with a summer move from Freiburg to Newcastle, instead delighted Villa fans and demonstrated why the club paid a record £50 million plus fee.  

The victory came at a time when Premier League CEO Richard Masters sat in the directors’ box, watching the two clubs most affected by the spending rules he has overseen. For Newcastle’s manager, Matthias Jaissle, the irony was stark: Manzambi’s goal sealed a dismal week for the Tynesiders.
summary: Johan Manzambi scored the winning goal for Aston Villa in their match against Newcastle. The 21-year-old Swiss midfielder had recently transferred from Freiburg to Villa for a record fee.

content:
Yehor Yarmolyuk’s red card fundamentally altered the Premier League match between Brentford and Liverpool, forcing Brentford to defend a 1-0 lead with ten men for the entire second half. title: Kartal battles past Ostapenko in Wuhan to secure spot in first WTA 1000 final
content:
Sonay Kartal defeated former French Open champion Jelena Ostapenko in straight sets on Saturday to advance to the final of the Wuhan Open, marking the biggest final of her career. The 24‑year‑old fought back from a deficit in both sets, winning 7‑6 (9), 7‑6 (5) after saving six set points.

Kartal’s victory comes in her second tour‑level tournament after a six‑month injury layoff. She entered the week ranked world No 170 due to recent inactivity, making her the lowest‑ranked player to reach a WTA 1000 final since the format began in 2009.

The win guarantees Kartal a jump into the world’s top 50 next week, overtaking Katie Boulter and becoming the new British No 1.
summary: Kartal battles past Ostapenko in Wuhan to secure spot in first WTA 1000 final.

title: Rising CPI to 3.7% in September adds pressure on GOP ahead of midterms
content: Recent economic data present a bleak outlook as early‑voting for the midterms proceeds, dealing another setback to Republicans. title: Federico Veronesi wins Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026; exhibit at NHM London
content:
The Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026 competition has announced its winners, presenting a selection of images that span subjects from underwater scenes to urban wildlife, photojournalism and mammal behaviour. The overall prize went to Italy’s Federico Veronesi for his striking photograph of an elephant carrying a dead calf.

All winning photographs will be displayed at London’s Natural History Museum, with the exhibition opening on 16 October 2026 and running through July 2027.
summary: The overall winner of the Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026 is Federico Veronesi of Italy for his image of an elephant carrying a dead calf. The winning photographs will be displayed at the Natural History Museum in London from 16 October 2026 until July 2027.

title: Scottish athlete Archie Goodburn meets Andy Burnham after TV brain cancer appeal
content: Scottish athlete Archie Goodburn, diagnosed two years ago with three inoperable brain tumours, delivered an emotional TV plea urging more investment in brain‑cancer research. After the appeal, he met with Andy Burnham, who responded to the call for increased funding.
summary: Scottish athlete Archie Goodburn, diagnosed with three inoperable brain tumours two years ago, made an emotional TV plea for more investment into brain cancer research. He later met Andy Burnham following the appeal.
